Newly metamorphosed glochidia of Quadrula quadrula begin their free-living existence at a remarkably small size. Upon release from the host fish, the settling juvenile bivalve possesses a shell length at settlement measuring just 0.03 centimeters . Even at the moment of birth, prior to the parasitic glochidial stage on a suitable fish host, the shell length at birth is only 0.02 centimeters [Lb = 0.02 centimeters]. This minute size at both parturition and settlement is typical of unionid mussels, which produce vast numbers of offspring to compensate for the high mortality associated with host-fish attachment and the subsequent transition to a benthic existence. The prodissoconch shell is fragile and translucent at these early stages, offering minimal protection from physical abrasion or predation. The veliger larva, once metamorphosed, must locate a suitable substratum quickly to begin its juvenile growth phase. The initiation of filter-feeding and siphonal development marks a critical energetic transition, allowing the juvenile to grow rapidly and escape the size window of highest vulnerability to benthic invertebrate predators.

As juvenile Quadrula quadrula grow and mature, significant developmental milestones define their transition toward adulthood. The species attains sexual maturity, or puberty, upon reaching a shell length at puberty of 5 centimeters [Lp = 5 centimeters], a size that typically corresponds to an age of several years in temperate river systems. Achieving this length represents a substantial investment in somatic growth from the sub-millimeter dimensions of the newly settled spat. In comparison to some other unionids, the ultimate shell length of this species has been documented as 11.05 centimeters [Li = 11.05 centimeters], a value derived from field measurements of the largest individuals encountered in stable, productive habitats. This adult body size places Quadrula quadrula among the medium-to-large freshwater mussels of North America. The transition from the juvenile to the adult reproductive stage involves not only an increase in shell dimension but also the maturation of the gonads, which become fully active only after the individual has reached this critical size threshold. Growth increments slow considerably after puberty, with most energetic resources being diverted toward gamete production rather than shell accretion.

At a stable water temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C], a sexually mature adult female with a shell length of 9.15 centimeters produces approximately 115,000 offspring per year [Ri = approximately 115,000 offspring per year]. This annual fecundity rate reflects the high fecundity typical of unionid mussels, which release large numbers of glochidia into the water column to maximize the probability of encountering a compatible host fish. The production of such vast numbers of larvae imposes a considerable energetic cost on the female, who must invest a substantial portion of the resources filtered from the water column into gametogenesis. This reproductive strategy, characterized by high fecundity and external larval brooding within the marsupial gill region, is consistent with a life history adapted to unpredictable host availability and high larval mortality in the planktonic or parasitic stage. The 17 °C [T = 17 °C] thermal regime under which these rates were measured corresponds to late spring or early autumn temperatures in many Midwestern rivers where the species occurs.

The early life history of Quadrula quadrula is closely tied to thermal conditions, which govern both the duration of brooding and the timing of glochidial release. Under laboratory conditions, the age at birth, defined as the interval from fertilization to the release of mature glochidia from the female's marsupial gills, is approximately 10 days [ab = approximately 10 days] when brooding females are maintained at 16 °C [T = 16 °C]. This relatively brief developmental period is consistent with the pattern observed in other members of the tribe Quadrulini, which tend to be short-term brooders (tachytictic) during the summer months. The developing embryos are retained within the gill chambers, where they are protected from predation and receive oxygenated water via the female's respiratory current. After these ten days, the larvae are expelled as fully developed glochidia, ready to attach to the gills or fins of a suitable fish host. The timing of this release is critical: it must coincide with the presence of the appropriate host species, which for Quadrula quadrula is believed to include certain ictalurid catfishes. Thus, a 10-day brooding period at 16 °C [T = 16 °C] (10 days) [ab = 10 days] represents a finely tuned reproductive phenology.

The complete lifespan of Quadrula quadrula, from the release of the glochidium to natural senescence and death, has been estimated from long-term mark-recapture studies and analysis of annual growth rings on the shell. The maximum recorded longevity for this species is 25 years [am = 25 years], based on individuals that completed their life cycle at 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. This impressive lifespan places Quadrula quadrula among the longer-lived freshwater mussels, a group renowned for its exceptional longevity relative to body size. The adult body mass associated with an individual that has attained its ultimate shell length of 11.05 centimeters is 47.9 grams [Wwi = 47.9 grams] of wet weight, reflecting the substantial soft-tissue biomass contained within the paired calcareous valves. This ultimate wet weight (47.9 grams) [Wwi = 47.9 grams] is consistent with a size-corrected allometric relationship observed in related unionid taxa, confirming the species' investment of resources in both shell growth and soft-tissue production. The combination of slow growth, late maturity, and a multi-decadal lifespan aligns Quadrula quadrula with a classic K-selected life-history strategy, rendering it particularly vulnerable to habitat degradation and overharvesting of host fish populations.
